content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I made a quick assessment of this paper.
content.review:
This paper presents a method for predicting method invocations in source code. The authors use an off-the-shelf NMT model to predict the method invocation at specific location. They show that their tool works reasonably well.

The application of this paper is interesting. However, I do not believe that ICLR is the appropriate venue for this work since it uses off-the-shelf phrase-based MT tool and a very simple representation to solve the problem. There is marginal novelty that relates to ICLR. Furthermore, the paper is badly written with multiple typos and lacks a rigorous evaluation.

* I would suggest to the authors to thoroughly spell and grammar-check this work. The grammar errors are too many to list here.

* Maybe the Mining Software Repositories is a better venue for this work, although I believe that it would still require significant improvements for it to be accepted there. https://2020.msrconf.org/track/msr-2020-papers#Call-for-Papers 

* The evaluation lacks any comparison with standard language models that have been employed in this field. A reasonable token-level language model (RNN/LSTM) would be necessary provide sufficient confidence that the representation method is useful.

* Data derived from scraping GitHub has been found to be very repetitive [a,b]. The authors are encouraged to check their corpus for duplicates.


Some Typos:

* "may be in the risk*s* of being" 
* "These challenges hinder*s*"
* "Can perform to predict the..." -> "can predict"

[a] Lopes, Cristina V., et al. "DéjàVu: a map of code duplicates on GitHub." Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages 1.OOPSLA (2017): 84.

[b] Allamanis, Miltiadis. "The Adverse Effects of Code Duplication in Machine Learning Models of Code." arXiv preprint arXiv:1812.06469 (2018).

content.title: Response to reviewer #2
content.comment:
First of all, thank you for your hard work in reviewing this paper. Your suggestions are very helpful to us.

We want to have some clarifications. In this work, we select SMT for 2 reasons. First, SMT training is flexible for users who did not have a GPU computer, to replicate our experiment results. Second, for this research (which source and target have the same length and no need to reorder translated result), the SMT is more flexible for altering the probability and get good accuracy. In this kind of parallel corpus, the SMT outperforms NMT in other problems in Diacritic Restoration in Natural Language Processing [3] and in Type inference (compare between [1] and [2]). Based on that, the main contribution of this work is for adapting and optimizing Statistical Machine Translation.

We know that the data by Github is repetitive. So, we apply some strategies for preparing the training corpus since our training corpus extracted from this repository. First, we select the highest stars project that used 6 libraries we mentioned in the evaluation. We do not select our projects developed mainly by some group of users or some organization, which reduces the risk of repetition. Second, we use the Github API, which allows users to avoid the “forked” projects. We wish to mention it in the paper in the extending version of the paper is accepted.

To better evaluate the approach, we conduct the external corpus collected from code snippets from Online Forums such as StackOverflow. We hired a developer to collect manually and we check that the code snippets are not duplicated. Since we use external data for testing the quality of the corpus by Github (section 3.2), the risk of repetition of Github affects the accuracy that can be avoided.

References:
[1]. https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8453132 
[2]. https://dl.acm.org/citation.cfm?id=3236051 
[3]. https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.07104

content.title: Thanks
content.comment:
Thank you for your response.

* I do not necessarily disagree that SMT is the "wrong" choice here. The problem I see in this work, as the other reviewers also note, is that the scope of the work is outside of this conference. Specifically, one would expect that a paper in a machine learning conference either uses a novel representation of data (but a sequence is used) and designs a new machine learning model/learning method or adapts existing ones to a new domain (an off-the-shelf tool is used). 

This work performs a few steps of data pre-processing and uses an off-the-shelf method. In itself, this may be valuable for the software engineering (research and practice) community, but it's not a contribution that is relevant to machine learning researchers and practitioners. For this reason, I still believe that this paper is not relevant to this community and should be rejected for ICLR. 

This is not necessarily a judgement of this work as a whole, but rather a judgement on the appropriateness of this work for ICLR/ machine learning conferences.

* Repetitiveness: One of the main findings of the DéjàVu work is that whole libraries are commonly copy-pasted in a repository, even in popular ones. In that sense, I would strongly encourage you to filter your corpus using some of the tools in [a] or [b]. External evaluation is indeed helpful, but removing duplicates may still improve your results (if we are to believe [b]).

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review:
This paper present a strategy to map the method name to method invocation. This contains several modules: a classifier module to classify the invocation by level of abstraction; A rule-based system to extract code; an algorithm to visit a method invocation inside the code environment; and finally a SMT system for predicting the sequences of AST (abstract syntax tree) structure given method name and content. I am not an expert on program synthesis, so I am evaluating this paper based on my educated guess, thus probably underestimate or miss some merits of this paper. I think the writing is clear and pedagogical, so that a non-expert reader can learn how such a system can be designed. However, although this task sounds interesting to me, this appears to me more like a system design paper rather than a typical top-notch machine learning paper. Specifically,

1. the technical innovations and the existing strategies are presented in a mixed way, rendering it quite difficult to clearly distinguish the novelty of this paper. 

2. Although I am not familiar with the evaluation metrics as presented in this paper, I feel that the judgements are rather subjective as no baselines are included in the comparison.

content.title: Response to reviewer #3
content.comment:
First of all, thank you for your hard work in reviewing this paper.

In our knowledge, our work is the first work that provided an approach for accepting a list of method names and other code elements as input and output as a list of ASTs of method invocations. For using machine translation to generate code, Deep API [1] is one of the research work that applies the Neural Machine Translation to suggest APIs from documentation of a method. However, the APIs outputted by Deep API just suggest to developers which types of APIs will be used, while our approach generates the complete ASTs of the code, which only require developers to add local variables to have the final code.

References:
[1] https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.08535

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I made a quick assessment of this paper.
content.review:
The paper proposes a code completion tool InvocMap, to predict nested method invocations in programming language code. 

I do not entirely buy the premise that "developers need to remember the structure and the combination of invocations depending on their purpose." which is stated as a reason for why the task is challenging. The order of nesting in method invocation can be resolved often by examining the return type and argument type(s) of each method.

Weaknesses
1. Writing can be improved significantly. It is hard to understand the difficulty of the problem that is being addressed.
2. Little novelty. A standard SMT approach is adopted with little modification. 
3. How is it ensured that the output is syntactically correct? 
4. Little analysis in the experiments, no strong baselines. Why not try a neural seq2seq model?

Typos/Grammar
1. There are two reasons "cause to" this challenge.
2.  First, large scale code corpus contains "noise" data

I am not entirely certain that this paper is appropriate for this venue.

content.title: Response to reviewer #1
content.comment:
First of all, we want to thank you for your feedback which is very helpful to authors. 
We want to make some comments. 

1. The reviewer is correct in the sense that experienced developers might be familiar with what types they need to return or types of arguments they need to use. We want to clarify 2 points. First, with non experienced developers, remembering types and arguments of method invocation are challenging. There are many types of research on automatically inferring the types of method invocations along with other programming elements, which shows the importance of this suggestion to developers [1,2]. Second, along with nested method invocation, there are other elements (Field Access, constructor) can appear inside the method invocation. In our approach, we do not only suggest the types of method invocations and its argument but also its AST structure, which can be complicated like example 1.a in the paper.

2. The main contribution of this paper is about adapting an SMT system for code generation. To make the SMT be able to get high accuracy, we rely on our theory of understand method invocations by abstraction levels and provide a parallel corpus that is aligned between source and target language. Each pair of source and target language have the same length of tokens and be consistent in order. To optimize the SMT for this type of corpus, we altering the alignment model which turns off the reordering probability which we mentioned in section 2.4. We wish to discuss more on this optimization but due to the recommended length of the paper, we just overview this part. 

3. The input of Machine Translation is the list of the method name and the output is the list of ASTs. In algorithms provided in section 2.4, we checked the AST encoded in the training dataset needs to be syntactically correct.   

4. In our knowledge, our work is the first work that integrated information of multiple abstracted method names to infer ASTs as complex method invocations. We select SMT over NMT thanks to two reasons. First, SMT training is flexible for users who did not have a GPU computer, to replicate our experiment results. Second, for this research (which source and target have the same length and no need to reorder translated result), the SMT is more flexible for altering the probability and get good accuracy. In this kind of parallel corpus, the SMT outperforms NMT in other problems in Diacritic Restoration in Natural Language Processing [3] and in Type inference (compare between [1] and [2]).

References:
[1]. https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8453132 
[2]. https://dl.acm.org/citation.cfm?id=3236051 
[3]. https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.07104
